453.t: Hearing Louis Armstrong's records and arranging his tunes
453.s: He had no night off to hear the river-boat bands, but knew Armstrong's Hot Five records and Snag It, made arrangements of Armstrong tunes, and was moved by the Bessie Smith St. Louis Blues record.
453.q: Unfortunately I didn't get a chance to get to the boats. No. Because playing at the theater I was playing every night, didn't have a night off. Then when I was at the Club I didn't have a night off.

453.t: Meeting Armstrong and proving he could read music
453.s: Randolph took a tune to Armstrong at the Regal, and Armstrong sang the difficult intervals at sight, convincing Randolph that the rumor he could not read was false.
453.q: I was teaching Lil. I met Louie when he came back to do a show at the Regal, and I went back and carried a tune that I had written. The title of my tune then was -- I'll think of it -- da-da-da-da-- 'I Don't Care What You

453.t: Armstrong's singing, his playing and what it was like working with him
453.s: Armstrong played the way he sang; playing with him every night was a ball, and he was a down-home man, not a distant leader.
453.q: Yeah. Louie -- I don't know -- that really was something else. He didn't have a beautiful voice, but there was something in it that you would like and I've been trying to find out what was it.

453.t: Letting Armstrong sleep rather than make a Washington broadcast
453.s: On a one-nighter run in Washington Randolph refused to wake Armstrong for a broadcast, angering Joe Glaser and Armstrong's wife Alpha.
453.q: I never will forget Louie -- we just got into a place in Washington, Washington, D.C., and Joe Glaser says, 'We're going to broadcast,' and I said, 'Louie just got in he's got his cot down, and he's and (unintelligible) going to sleep.' He said, 'Well, he'll have to get up because we're going to…

453.t: Armstrong's habits on the road and the Louis and Lil stage act
453.s: Armstrong did not jam after work but went to bed; Randolph praises the immaculate comic act of Louis and Lil in a New Orleans theater.
453.q: No, he didn't do any of that, no. No, because Louis worked so devilish hard, when he got through, he'd go and hit the sack.

453.t: Song choices and Sleepytime Down South as theme
453.s: Randolph says Armstrong simply liked the Southern-flavored songs, not a managed image, recalls the press reaction to his Yes, Lord and notes Sleepytime as his theme.
453.q: when he made "Sleepytime Down South," and he says, "Yes, Lord," and they jumped on it because he made an expression like that.

453.t: I Wonder Who, the Laughin' Louie record and loose studio sessions
453.s: They try to identify a tune from Laughin' Louie and discuss the humor and relaxed atmosphere of the sessions with Armstrong keeping everyone laughing.
453.q: Yes, they really was. Yes certainly -- you know, usually, recording sessions, you'd get tense, sometimes, when the red light -- especially when the red light come on. It'd be all right, long as you're just taking it down for the timing, and so, you'd say, all right, quiet, the red light come on and…

453.t: Staying back on You Can Depend On Me and Armstrong's Lionel Hampton record
453.s: Randolph played the background trumpet softly because Armstrong, remembering how he had held down Lionel Hampton on a Les Hite record, wanted him to stay back.
453.q: But when he says, Randy, I'm going to play a record for you. This was down at New Orleans, and he played some record that when he was with Les Hite's band, and Lionel was playing the vibes. And he says, now, you're going to have to listen real hard to hear this, he says, because of the fact, he…

453.t: The 1933 book, and Armstrong is the whole band
453.s: The book mixed arrangements, heads and stocks; Armstrong told him not to be bothered by people saying he was the whole band, and they talked music and the Saints.
453.q: Yeah, he was the star attraction. No, the only thing, he did say to me, he told me, he said, don't let -- people that was saying that about this first band, now, this was the first band. He told me, don't let this worry you, but the people say that Louis Armstrong is the whole band, and he told me,…

453.t: Did Armstrong's chops ever come back after 1934?
453.s: DeMichael hears less brilliance in the 1935 Russell records; Randolph saw Armstrong still picking at his lip with a mirror and agrees.
453.q: Because I know -- I used to see him all the time, he'd carry a little mirror, and I used to see him all the time with that little mirror, looking at the -- and picking at his --

453.t: Armstrong's work pace, and the band that would not back him up
453.s: Randolph says the men did not support him; leaving New Orleans for Little Rock in 1934 he went door to door rousting late sidemen.
453.q: Yes, he worked pretty hard. And -- something, though, I really believe that when Louis said we're going to run this band -- say, Randolph will run the band -- run it in the ground, and said, if he does that Louis Armstrong was going in the ground with them. I think that the men didn't back us up.…

453.t: Armstrong as supreme improviser, I Can't Give You Anything But Love
453.s: Both agree Armstrong was the greatest melodic improviser with form; Randolph points to his I Can't Give You Anything But Love as an eye-opener.
453.q: He certainly did. And you know what really brought that out, what opened my eyes on that? I guess you heard it too, is, 'I Can't Give You Anything But Love.'

453.t: Idolizing Armstrong after five years with him
453.s: Randolph can imitate Armstrong's voice and horn, was with him nearly five years and ranks him just behind God and his wife.
453.q: And that gravel voice Louis got. But you know, I can imitate Louis so -- and the way he blows his trumpet, his singing and his talking. Well, I should, I was with the man right up on five years and I idolized the man.

453.t: Armstrong's path from 1929 to the April 1931 band, and who joined when
453.s: DeMichael reviews Armstrong's years with Dickerson, New York and Les Hite and his 1931 arrest; Randolph and Lindsay were added to an existing band, and he was not in the band for the Showboat trouble.
453.q: This band -- this band to my knowing never got to the Regal. No, this band never got to the Regal because Collins was the manager of Louie and Collins pulled Louie out from the band in New York and sent us back home and sent Louie over in France.

453.t: Armstrong's welcome in New Orleans and hearing Louis Prima
453.s: A Black crowd lifted Armstrong on arrival and the band stayed at Patterson's Hotel; Randolph heard a band singing in Armstrong's manner and it was Louis Prima.
453.q: It was. They had -- it was very good, and the last I remember seeing Louis, the crowd picked him up, and Louis was kicking -- that was comical.

453.t: Comparing the 1931, 1933 and 1934 Armstrong bands
453.s: The 1931 band was almost a combo of about ten, the 1933 band was cleaner, and DeMichael thinks the 1934 band had the most interesting arrangements.
453.q: Yes, had the trumpet. Let's see, the '33 had -- before we joined, they had only Louis -- there was nine pieces, three sax and four rhythm.

453.t: Armstrong gives Glaser the reins; the union deal and end of the band
453.s: After the lateness Armstrong told Glaser he had full say over the band, and then the union arrangement brought Luis Russell in and let go the whole band.
453.q: And he was going to be with me, if I run the band in the ground, Louis Armstrong was going in the ground with the band. Well, then he had come back to Joe and told Joe now you got full rein with the band.

453.t: Trumpet solos on records and Armstrong featuring Whitlock in Louisville
453.s: Armstrong rarely featured other trumpeters on records, but at dances he featured Stump Whitlock, especially in Whitlock's hometown of Louisville.
453.q: Well, Louis -- now, playing in the recordings, to be perfectly they played with the Frank, Recording, Louis didn't feature too many trumpeters.

453.t: Picking the musicians for the 1933 band
453.s: Randolph chose the Oldham boys and Mike McKendrick sent in trumpeter Stump Whitlock, after Armstrong wired both of them.
453.q: picked some. I picked the Olden boys. Mike McKendrick had -- he sent in that little fellow by the name of Stump Whitlock.

453.t: Joining Armstrong in Detroit in 1931 and who assembled the band
453.s: Randolph joined at the Greystone Ballroom in June 1931 and, asked whether he selected the men, names George James, Al Washington, Tubby Hall, Johnny Lindsay and Preston Jackson.
453.q: I arranged -- well, you see, I don't know how to get that straight, but, now -- how many bands did I get together for him? Now, this band was -- the band broke up, I did get the band together for him. Yeah, I did put -- one, two, three -- let's see, George James and Al Washington.

453.t: Armstrong tells him on opening night: this is your band
453.s: On the Greystone opening night Armstrong made Randolph take the band, embarrassing him when he stomped off seated, and he then directed sets whenever Armstrong rested.
453.q: Now, to really to get your -- to get the record straight about -- now, this band -- I joined Louie starting in Detroit. I made a jump out here -- this man, Johnny Lindsay and myself, see -- see, we joined Louie. I'll tell you why I'm sitting over there after awhile and not sitting here. I joined…

87.t: First seeing Louis Armstrong at the Howard Theater
87.s: He saw Armstrong in Washington about 1930, once giving him a knife for a corn; Armstrong later said he overblew then.
87.q: I remember when I first saw Louis when he came through Washington, this was about 1930, somewhere around that time. I'd heard him a lot on records, but when I first got to really see him good was in Washington. He came there. He had -- at the Howard Theater -- he had -- he used to cut his hair in a…

87.t: What he learned from Louis about preserving himself
87.s: Watching Armstrong, Young learned to rest, not eat a big meal before playing, and not play too many high choruses at rehearsal.
87.q: No, Louis wouldn't have played that many high choruses at a rehearsal. He might have played one to see if he was in good shape, but he would have played the

87.t: Leaving Louis Armstrong because his wife was ill
87.s: After 12 years with Armstrong, he left in 1964 to care for his wife, who had cancer, and Joe Glaser was angry.
87.q: : So, yeah, I stayed with Louis until '64, and this is -- well, I knew my wife was sick, but I didn't know what was wrong with her. I'd bought a home in the meantime here in Los Angeles, and her and my daughter were living here. So I just would commute. You know, when I had told you how much time…

87.t: Louis's understanding and generosity
87.s: Armstrong later understood in Honolulu, and Young says he was warm and generous without wanting publicity.
87.q: Oh, yeah, sure. That's right. But -- and, you know, he never -- he hardly ever spoke to me again after that. But Louis was all right. He could understand. Louis had a heart. You know, he had a big heart, because he came to Honolulu later on, and he called me up to his room, you know, after work. I…

87.t: Louis keeping him up to coach Tyree Glenn; learning from Armstrong
87.s: Armstrong kept Young up all night in Honolulu to teach Tyree Glenn the vocal spots; Young learned timing and phrasing from him.
87.q: He kept me up all night. Louis didn't like to sleep, for one thing. I tell you something about Louis. Louis and Duke had similar qualities. They always want people around them. And Louis didn't -- he didn't like to sleep, so he called me up, and he had me with him all night to show Tyree Glenn how…

87.t: The Goodman-Armstrong tour and showmanship
87.s: Benny Goodman put Armstrong on first, then last on John Hammond's advice, and complained of clowning; Young says Louis was both musician and showman.
87.q: I tell you something that happened when I was with Louis. We had a tour with Benny Goodman and Benny Goodman's big band, and so Benny had some money put up in the tour. Joe Glaser's office was booking it. And so they decided to put -- Benny decided to put Louis on first. You know, that old show…

87.t: What Young learned: timing, building a solo, stage presentation
87.s: From Armstrong he learned to build slowly, relax on stage and read an audience.
87.q: I don't know. I would say I learned a lot about timing from Louis. I learned a lot about building, like not starting out too strong, just building things and, you know, starting easy and building things up. And these things are important.

87.t: Traveling first class with Louis; his bad heart
87.s: Armstrong's tours were hard but first class; he had heart trouble and a heart attack at Spoleto.
87.q: He did, but it was hard. I'll tell you something about one-nighters. I don't care how you do them, they're hard. But at least it was first class, the way we traveled with Louis. It was -- it was rough, but it was first class.

87.t: Louis's and Duke's itineraries and Glaser's favoritism
87.s: Willard compares Armstrong's lighter itineraries with Ellington's; Duke complained Glaser gave Louis better dates.
87.q: We used to do it. But when Louis started getting sick, then he started lightening up on them. We used to do the same thing.

87.t: How Joe Glaser became Louis's manager
87.s: Louis fired his manager Collins after John Hammond knocked Collins down for a slur, and asked Glaser to take over.
87.q: Louis told me the story himself. Louis had a manager by the name of Collins, and from what I can gather, he was a big crook, you know.

87.t: Glaser's handshake deal and handling Louis's money
87.s: They never had a contract, and Glaser kept Louis's money safe, leaving him and Lucille millions.
87.q: So finally Louis talked him into being his -- they never did have a contract. They shook hands. For 45 years he was his manager, only on a handshake. And Glaser, on the strength of being with Louis, Louis used to tell us stories about it. They used to ride the bus down South with Glaser, and Glaser…

87.t: Glaser and Louis depended on each other; Glaser managing Duke
87.s: Glaser cared about Louis and died shortly before him; Young was glad Glaser's office also got Duke lucrative work.
87.q: He's giving everybody else a royal -- what you call 'em, you know -- so it made no difference what they thought of him. He knew how he and Louis stood.

87.t: Louis as adviser to statesmen; staying with Tshombe
87.s: Young marvels that world leaders consulted Armstrong, who scolded Tshombe, and the band feared for his safety at Tshombe's house.
87.q: Well, it was a different scene with him and Duke and him and Louis. You can understand why he cared more for Louis than he did anybody. But everybody around that office knew that. They knew that Joe cared more for Louis than he did for his own family. He wasn't very close to his family in Chicago,…

87.t: Louis's replies to the press in Beirut and Cairo
87.s: Asked why he would play for Israel, Louis said a note is a note in any language; in Cairo he told reporters he had a trumpet and a young wife.
87.q: Louis was -- I ever tell you about some of the interviews Louis had over there in -- oh, man, we played with -- we went to Beirut with Louis. So these guys who booked us down in Beirut, these two brothers, George and -- I forget

87.t: Ernie Anderson, the Pope, and Doc Pugh
87.s: Publicist Ernie Anderson tells how Louis answered the Pope's question about children, and Louis's quip about his valet Doc Pugh's death.
87.q: Well, Ernie Anderson used to be the PR man for -- he loved Louis all his life. In fact, he's the guy set up Nixkin the Village and all those -- Eddie Condons and all, because he loved jazz. But he's a brainy guy. He lives in London, and he's PR man. So Ernie hung around us all the time. And Ernie,…

87.t: Louis's constant humor
87.s: Young says Armstrong's quips came off the top of his head and kept him in stitches.
87.q: -- you could go on all night telling stories about this guy, and that's the kind of guy he was, man. One guy said, hey, Louis, how's everything going? He said, hey, Daddy, white folks still in the lead. He kept on walking.

87.t: Louis on modern paintings at the Louvre
87.s: Armstrong told Young the Russians put the modern paintings up to confuse Americans.
87.q: -- he told me one day -- I never forgot this. He said -- it was in Paris, and some people had just took us down to Louvre, you know, to see all --

87.t: Princess Margaret, Prince Akihito, the "black Buddha" and the catcher's mitt
87.s: Stories of Armstrong holding court with royalty, dancing with the Japanese princess, and wearing a catcher's mitt to protect his lip.
87.q: I couldn't believe things that he used to tell me, like funny, man. But, yeah, we go in Europe, and here's Princess Margaret and all of them like that, asking him about -- questions about things, and he's sitting up there having court with these big people.

87.t: Armstrong's congestion and daily laxative
87.s: Armstrong coughed constantly, slept in a fan's draft, and took Pluto Water then Swiss Kriss every night, per his doctor.
87.q: His -- he had a bad congestion problem. He used to cough hard all the -- for years, years and years. He coughed hard all the time. But he used to do some of the damndest things. He'd eat a big meal over there in Italy, and he'd get on a great big fan and go get in a chair and lay back and go to…

87.t: Louis's musical directors and rehearsing for TV
87.s: Armstrong rarely rehearsed bands himself; Billy Kyle and earlier Joe Garland and Louis Russell handled it.
87.q: I think Louie was playing in front of Louis Russell's group, Louis Russell's group, at that time. Of course, Louie had a lot of bands of his own back at that time, but if I'm not -- I'm not sure, but I'm pretty -- I think he was fronting Louis Russell's band at that time. You see, Louis never did…

9.t: Hoagy Carmichael, 'Rockin' Chair' and Armstrong's genius
9.s: Armstrong accepted any tune brought into the studio, leaving Russell to make arrangements, and Holmes calls him a genius.
9.ch: Luis Russell's Nest Club band, 1928-30
9.q: : That happened with "Mahogany Hall Stomp" and "Old Rockin' Chair". Hoagy Carmichael walked in. "Louis, I want you to do this (?). Can you record this for me?" [POPS' VOICE] "Yeah, man. Yeah, man." He'd never say no. He'd

9.t: Sylvester Lewis and the tape proving he was a musician
9.s: He recalls Sy Oliver and trumpeter Sylvester Lewis, who after a USO tour worked in the subway and borrowed a tape to prove to co-workers he had led a band.
9.ch: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
9.q: : Sy Oliver. Even Sy Oliver. He was crazy about me, believe me. I was one of his favorite saxophone men. I don't even have a picture of anything with him. And a lot of people, they don't know I even worked with the man! I worked with him plenty. Sy Oliver... I don't have a photograph or anything.…

9.t: Louis Metcalf's crown and Armstrong's high F at the Savoy
9.s: Metcalf wore a crown as king of the band until Armstrong played a high F on a two-night Savoy visit and Teddy Hill threw the crown into the audience.
9.ch: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
9.q: : Louis had a crown made. Louis Metcalf had a crown. He was the king. That's because Russell had so many show-stopping numbers we used to play, and naturally, we'd finish one of them numbers and the applause would bring the house down, as they say. Well, naturally, the trumpet player, he'd take the…

9.t: Coming and going with Russell, then five years with Armstrong
9.s: He left and rejoined Russell freely, and from 1935 to 1940 worked with Armstrong, finally unable to take the hard work.
9.ch: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
9.q: Yeah. I did. He was always glad when I come back. And usually I was glad to get back, too. They say the grass is always greener on the other side of the street -- until you get there.

9.t: The violins on 'Song of the Islands'
9.s: Asked about violinists added to an Armstrong record, Holmes sees nothing remarkable in it.
9.ch: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
9.q: Well, now, I guess everything is somebody's idea, you know. Maybe it was as big a surprise to him as it was to me. I mean, you know, it was nice... But it didn't make no records...it didn't break any records for makin' records. Just another nice (?).

9.t: Joe Glaser on the road and two quarts of whiskey at the Club Panama
9.s: Glaser rode the bus the first year and told clubs to give the band anything; in Chicago Holmes took him at his word and got sick.
9.ch: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
9.q: : No. He would come around. The first year he went out with us. The first year, he was in the bus with us. He was a forty-year-old manager, you know; he was forty during them days. He was good in this kind of way. We'd be in place where we couldn't get served, and he would, like, get out of the bus…

9.t: An eight-hundred-mile drive and Armstrong playing hard regardless
9.s: A Chicago-to-engagement run turned out to be eight hundred miles, and Armstrong still blew everyone off the stand on arrival.
9.ch: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
9.q: Into the bus, and four hundred more miles, or five or six or seven or eight hundred miles. We left Chicago one morning, we thought we was going six hundred miles to the next engagement. And when we got on the road and the road manager looked at the contract, we found out it was eight hundred miles…

9.t: Armstrong never knew where the band was playing and slept on buses
9.s: Armstrong left all band business to Russell and Glaser and slept soundly on the bus while Holmes could not.
9.ch: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
9.q: : Louis got up there and blew his horn. He had nothin' to say to the band as far as running the band was concerned. He wasn't interested in what the band's business was. Luis Russell was running the band...and Joe Glaser. Joe Glaser run everything. See, all the orders come from Joe Glaser. And…

9.t: Talking back to Glaser and being hard to get along with
9.s: Holmes was one of two band members never fired because he talked back, and says he walks away when he is unhappy.
9.ch: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
9.q: But see, I used to talk back to Joe. And you know, it was only about two people in that band that didn't get fired. And I was one of them, and Louis Bacon was another. He was another one would...he would bass right back at Joe

9.t: Armstrong forgets to introduce him at Boston's Symphony Hall
9.s: Armstrong usually introduced hometown players, but Russell had to remind him at Boston's Symphony Hall before he called Holmes 'Pickles'.
9.ch: Harlem venues and bandmates remembered
9.q: Well, he would always introduce... In anybody's home town we went to, he would always introduce this person to the audience, and let them know that one of

9.t: Armstrong gave Red Allen an hour of his own
9.s: Armstrong let Red Allen's own book fill an hour, then returned with one note that brought the house down.
9.ch: Harlem venues and bandmates remembered
9.q: Yeah, Louis was not the type to hold anybody back. If you could do anything, he'd let you do it, and he'd be glad to promote you. In fact, he wanted that very much. Do something, do it, and do it good. Just like with Red Allen... Red Allen was a great trumpet player in the band, and a lot of people…

9.t: Ready to pan Armstrong, who hit high F and called him Pickles
9.s: Russell's band was ready to pan Armstrong, but he dethroned Metcalf with big high notes; Armstrong always gave people nicknames, calling Holmes 'Pickles'.
9.ch: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
9.q: : That was just like... When Louis come, we was ready to pan Louis! You know? See, that's why... Somebody asked me once, didn't I get a big thrill when I found out I was going to be working with Louis Armstrong. I said, "Big thrill for what? We was gettin' ready to pan him!" We was gettin' ready to…

9.t: Rupert Cole joins Armstrong's band and loses at blackjack
9.s: Cole came from Don Redman's band, sight-read Armstrong's hard book as lead alto, won at blackjack on his first night and never again.
9.ch: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
9.q: Oh, Rupert Cole, alto player, clarinetist. He was a very good musician. He joined the band, I don't know exactly when, what the date was, he had some pretty stiff music to put in front of him when he joined the band.

9.t: The Lenox Club breakfast dance where Armstrong threw Rex Stewart's horn away
9.s: After Armstrong's Savoy appearance, musicians jammed at the Lenox Club's Sunday breakfast dances, and Armstrong outplayed Rex Stewart and Jack Teagarden.
9.ch: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
9.q: The Lenox Club was a nice little nightclub, an intimate spot in Harlem in the Roarin' Twenties. It used to be the home of... Well, I don't know. But it was a nice little place. It was not a big place. It was a small place, a small club.

9.t: Armstrong's broad tone and winning over unknowing Southern crowds
9.s: Armstrong's tone grew broader as he climbed, and he won over audiences who knew nothing of him while touring the South.
9.ch: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
9.q: : No. No, who would remember the number? He was just blowin', and in that big pretty tone. See, the thing that Louis had on everybody else... Most trumpet players, the higher they go, the thinner the tone got, and they would end up just squeaking, like a flute. But with Louis, the higher he went,…

9.t: Armstrong the hardest-working leader
9.s: Armstrong sweated through each dance, changed with no dressing room, and worked harder than any leader Holmes knew, unlike Lionel Hampton.
9.ch: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
9.q: : But he worked hard. Louis always worked hard. And boy, the perspiration would just run off of him. Oh brother, he worked awful hard. When he finished playing a dance, he had to strip down and change everything. And I mean, you see, places did not have them fine dressing rooms and showers and…

9.t: Joe Garland takes over with strict rules and uniform changes
9.s: Garland took over, posted uniform changes and made the reed section rehearse between shows; the band improved but the work felt like a factory.
9.ch: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
9.q: Well, two days later, he sent for us to come to rehearsal. Joe Garland's going to take over the band. Joe Garland? Man, he was the last one to come in here. And he's gonna take over? Well, I thought that was kind of funny, you know, the last man to come in the band. But I said didn't say nothin'.…

9.t: Russell caught between the band and Glaser, and giving up leadership
9.s: Glaser had Russell fire men on the word of job-seekers; Russell tired of the hatred and resigned, and nobody in the band wanted to take over.
9.ch: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
9.q: Well, he was the boss when... See, Russell was tired of the way things was run, and he was in the middle. Russell was in the middle between the band and Joe Glaser. Russell was catching hell from the men in the band plus Joe Glaser.

9.t: Condon, Mezzrow and Armstrong's hangers-on in the studio
9.s: Eddie Condon, Mezz Mezzrow and others followed Armstrong to every record date, so the studio held more bystanders than band members.
9.ch: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
9.q: : Yeah, he was... Well, he was in the studio every time Pops was. He was in the studio. You know what I mean? Yeah, he was the studio every time Pops made a record. Not only him, all his boys. Oh, there was a bunch of them. Mezz Mezzrow, you know, the Reefer King? Yeah, he was there. All them boys.…

9.t: Johnny Dunn and the French horn mix-up
9.s: Holmes remembers Johnny Dunn as a publicity-heavy trumpeter whose reign was over by 1927, and admits he is unobservant about how brass instruments are built.
9.ch: Musicians, gear and Armstrong recollections
9.q: : Well, Johnny Dunn was about... He was a sensation. He's the one had the publicity, the big note and the long horn, the long coach horn. And he was the king of the valves.

They tell you, “You should have come here Thursday.” Thursday was payday. You come here on Saturday and Sunday or Monday, ain’t…

If you get on the river, you see the river bends. So that’s a perfect ama . . . How you say that? There’s a word. Not atmosphere. It’s another word…

1.s: Jones's chordal variations influenced Armstrong, the two later drifted apart, and Jones joined the Missourians.

(inaudible)] or this plain. David Jones was running changes, and that’s . . . but he was a finished musician. David…

1.t: Louis Armstrong walks into Warrick Hall
1.s: At the one-night dance Armstrong appeared, Barker handed him a local trumpeter's horn and Armstrong played When You're Smiling, angering the horn's owner.
1.q: That was the first time I saw him in person. I’d heard of him. You saw his picture all over the place. It was just like you knew him, because my uncle Paul knew him. You understand? Louis claimed Paul was his best drummer he worked with. Paul used to get on his horse behind him. Them drums. Had a…

1.s: Danny and Milt recall Louis keeping a roll of cash for people in need, including old friends like John Foster and Stump Crouch.

76.t: Hiring Louis Armstrong for the Orchard Cabaret
76.s: Zutty hired Louis, Johnny St. Cyr and Yudell Wilson for the Orchard; Bootsy Hernandez, a Manuel Perez fan, loved Louis. Zutty says Louis played very well.
76.ch: New Orleans bands, Louis and the Lyric
76.q: And then I heard Louis was in town and I went and hired Louis Armstrong and I hired Johnny Sincere and St. Cyr Yudell Wilson.

76.t: Shy young Louis Armstrong on the boat
76.s: Marge met a shy Louis Armstrong on Marable's boat, who ran from the girls to the water fountain; Zutty adds he collected gum wrappers and spilled his olives in the station.
76.ch: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
76.q: He was the man, see he was the king, you know. Did the whole season on the St. Paul and took it to dry dock in Iowa with Charlie, so then when we came back to St. Louis that's when the work first started, just coming in. I hadn't even met Zutty then. Because Zutty wasn't on the boat, I was on the…

76.t: Naming the records: West End Blues and Knee Drops
76.s: Dance asks about the meaning of titles; Zutty says Knee Drops and Knocking the Jug were named in the studio, and Louis was thrilled to see his name in lights at the Savoy.
76.q: With Kaiser Marshall. Teagarden, he's on there also. See because that's when Louis from the play at the Savoy. That's when he made those records. He told me, he said, Zutty he said, man, they had my name in lights at the Savoy, you know. Louis Armstrong, you know. And that knocked him out.

76.t: Louis the humble man, and his last days in hospital
76.s: Marge says Louis stayed down to earth, amazed at the limousine, and was closest to Zutty. In his last days Louis asked for Zutty at the hospital, where they sat with him.
76.q: Well I always say that, there's maybe one thing I can say, maybe Louis got commercial. But Louis was still a humble man. He was really an earth man to the very end. He told Zuddy when come and pick him up and take him he was going to take him to the Carson Show. And he said, yes man, he said, you…

76.t: The private tape of Louis and Zutty reminiscing
76.s: Louis and Zutty made a private tape at the Alvin Hotel where he talked about Punch Miller, and Louis played Zutty's records and told his chauffeur how Zutty could push a band.
76.q: Well that's something else. He tells about Punch Miller in that tape. (LAUGHTER). He let Punch Miller right on that tape. He made it himself. Lucille doesn't have that tape. Nobody has that tape. It was made in the Alvin Hotel on Louis' last go round. He and Zutty were talking about old times.

76.t: Filling in for Ellington at the Audubon Theatre
76.s: In New York the band first opened at the Savoy, then took Duke's place at the Audubon Theatre in the Bronx, where Louis's St. Louis Blues high notes made the pit orchestra stand up.
76.ch: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
76.q: Well we first opened at the Savoy here in New York City. Because I sent Marge a telegram saying, breaking Savoy up. Then we got a job to play in Duke's place at the Audobon Theater. And that's when they had the big band in the pit and Louis played the 'St. Louis Blues and hit them high ones. And…

76.t: Louis, Zutty and the choice between friendship and business
76.s: Louis asked Zutty to stay with him, but Zutty had a Connie's Inn offer and told Louis friendship is one thing and business another; Mezz's book says he cut out from Louis.
76.ch: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
76.q: Yes. Oh way after, yes. And so Louis told me how much money he had a chance to make and everything like that. And that's when I told Louis, I said, well Louis, friendship is one thing and business is another. See, but Mezz put it in his book that I was cutting out from Louis. But Marge knows that…

76.t: Joe Glaser opens the Sunset and bills Louis the World's Greatest Trumpeter
76.s: Back in Chicago Zutty was doubling with Doc Cook while Joe Glaser opened the Sunset and first billed Louis Armstrong as World's Greatest Trumpeter.
76.ch: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
76.q: Because we doubled, you know, we were doubling see, and in the mean time Joe Glaser opened the Sunset. And he was the first one to put Louis' name, 'World's Greatest Trumpeter'. He was the first one to hang that notice, to do that. Yes.

76.t: Hot Chocolates: Louis keeps Zutty at Connie's Inn
76.s: Dance says Hot Chocolates and Ain't Misbehavin' marked Louis's commercial rise; Zutty was wanted for the Broadway show but Louis told him to stay and take care of the Connie's Inn band.
76.ch: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
76.q: Of course they wanted me to play the show on Broadway, Hot Chocolates. But Louis said no, he wanted me to stay to take care of the band at the Inn. See, so I got cut out of that. Because they really, the producer Leonard Harper and all, they wanted me to play that show on Broadway. See, 'Aint…

76.t: Lucille's claim that Zutty took a band from Louis
76.s: Marge reports Lucille said Louis never hired Zutty because he would not have another band taken from him; Marge and Dance insist the Dickerson band simply broke up and Zutty stayed at Connie's Inn.
76.ch: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
76.q: And Now I can tell it the way Louis told Lucille you know when Zutty never worked with Louis any more you know and he never got Zutty in the band. And Lucille told me when we were out there spending the four days with her and she and I were downstairs talking you know. And she said, well you know…

76.t: Hot Chocolates and Connie's Inn: the shows and Louis's jealousy
76.s: Zutty played in pit bands, not as soloist; Louis did the Broadway show then returned to Connie's Inn, singing Black and Blue. Marge says friends believed Louis was jealous of Zutty's popularity with the show girls.
76.ch: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
76.q: But personally there was a little jealousy in those days with Louis. And that's what Barney (Bonnie?) says all the time, Louis was jealous you know. And Pop Foster says the same thing. And EARVELL SHAW says the same thing you know and all. But the show girls, the dancing girls, the acts the hits,…

76.t: Zutty would have quit any band to play with Louis; Louis's devotion
76.s: Marge says Zutty would have given up anything to play with Louis, who loved him back and nursed him after his stroke, saying he'd kill himself if Zutty died.
76.ch: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
76.q: He always had that you know. Now Zutty, Zutty had his bands and everything. His little outfits you know. He had, but he would have quit any of them to play with Louis Armstrong. Zutty just loved Louis. He just loved Louis. He wanted to play with Louis. And he'd have given up anything to play with…

76.t: Zutty never recorded with Louis except Dickerson and Chicago sessions
76.s: They agree Zutty never made a full record date with Louis other than the Carroll Dickerson band, When You're Smiling, and the Chicago small-group sides such as Skip the Gutter and Knee Drops.
76.ch: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
76.q: Oh yes. Well we made that 'When you're Smiling'. That was part of the band. And like those things I did with Louis in Chicago.

76.t: Lil Armstrong and Rockwell steer Louis toward money
76.s: Marge says Lil wanted Louis to commercialize, and was unhappy to see them the night Zutty confronted Louis; Lil said she would straighten the record in her book but never did.
76.ch: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
76.q: And Lil was a big influence. She would commercialize Louis too you know. She loved Zutty, Lille did. But I know when Rockwell told him how much money he could make, and I know Lil was for that you know. Naturally, because when we went down there that night Lil didn't look like she was too happy to…

76.t: The Luis Russell band behind Louis
76.s: Marge says Russell's was the worst band, unlike Dickerson's, whose men played like a choir behind Louis; at Loew's State Louis told Zutty he did not even hear them.
76.ch: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
76.q: No. It was the worst band you ever heard. That's why Zutty told him, Louis one night, he said, I don't see, we went down to Loew's State to hear him when Louis was directing the band. And Zutty told Louis when he had him up to the house for dinner and Zutty said, how can you play with such a bad…

76.t: Louis leaves Dickerson's band and joins Luis Russell
76.s: Louis left Connie's Inn and the Dickerson band without warning, leaving the men stranded and short of fare to Chicago, and joined Luis Russell's band, booked by Rockwell.
76.ch: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
76.q: Jimmy Strong, he was up to our house crying because he hardly had fare to get back to Chicago. And so many of them they didn't even have the fare back to Chicago. But Zutty was all set because when Louis cut out from Connie's Inn, Louis wanted Zutty out of that band.

76.t: Show people at the Nest, and Louis and Hines opening the Sunset
76.s: Zutty names theatrical visitors, including Carl Sandburg; King Oliver wanted Louis at the Plantation but Louis opened at the Sunset across the street, with Earl Hines.
76.ch: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
76.q: Yes Ravel and Paul Sandburg he used to come up there a lot. Yes because he was good friends with Nora Ray Holt and that other gal, what was her name Marge that sang and became and entertained at the Apex? You know her husband passed away.

76.t: Louis in Chick Webb's band and the sore lip
76.s: After Russell, Louis went with Chick Webb's band, which was wrong for him, with jealous trumpeters, and strain on his lip from nightly high notes forced him to lay off for about a year.
76.ch: Chicago and New York with Louis Armstrong, 1925-30
76.q: No that didn't last long because they made his lip sore. See they weren't right with him at all. That band had him going so. That's when he had to lay off about a year because of the sore lip. He laid off a long time with that sore lip. Because that band made his lip sore.

124.t: Lil Armstrong's Midwest tour and breakup
124.s: Green booked the band across the Midwest and Kentucky; it disbanded in Lexington and Lil went to New York.
124.ch: Depression gigs, Lil Armstrong, joining Chick Webb
124.q: And Charlie called me and say, "Well bring all the guys back to New York, because Lil Armstrong is not coming back out again," you know.

124.t: Louis Armstrong's "Sit Down, You're Rockin' the Boat" date
124.s: McRae helped engineer an Armstrong date where the Sy Oliver arrangements had not been delivered, and they discuss Armstrong's schooling.

124.q: But getting back to the sound, we recorded Louie over there. I engineered with them when Louie did "Sit Down You Rock The Boat." year that That (inaudible) Louie had that small band. And Louie came in to do a date, and he wanted me to come over to the studio and meet him.

124.s: Glaser sent McRae to hear Armstrong's old band in Roanoke; later McRae replaced a drinking brass section.

124.q: I did the same thing when I did it with Louie Armstrong. With Louie, I built Louie a complete new band. That was a different type of thing.

Now Jack would come -- and it was Jack (inaudible) Glaser. (chuckles) Jack would come with these two fine chicks on his…

124.t: Building Armstrong's new band and becoming musical director
124.s: Joe Glaser wanted a younger band for Louis Armstrong, whose old band was losing men, and put McRae in charge.
124.ch: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
124.q: And then when I came back, Glaser had still wanted me to go out -- I was (inaudible). Called me up one day -- he wanted me -- I was still writing. I say I come back to writing and stuff, but then I picked -- Sid Wyche and I started doing some writing together. Still writing these rock and roll…

124.t: Music director for Armstrong; the command performance joke
124.s: Armstrong left everything to McRae, including a command performance where he stopped the band on air, joking he wanted McRae's name broadcast.
124.ch: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
124.q: I did more there than I did with Chick, because Louie was a different type of man that Chick was, you know. You had to do everything. You had to call all the rehearsals, tell him what time you're gonna leave -- he didn't wanna know. Louie didn't want nothing. He was just -- this was Louie Armstrong…

124.t: Bill Robinson and Louis Armstrong as deep thinkers
124.s: McRae finds both men gentle, thoughtful behind their showman faces.
124.ch: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
124.q: That's the kind of guy. He was -- just like nothing. Louie was more like Bill Robinson than anybody I worked with. Now there's a man with a beautiful mind, Bill Robinson. You never know -- See, it's a funny thing about a person. You never know them till you work with them. Bill Robinson was a great…

124.t: Rehearsing "Don't Fence Me In" late at night
124.s: Armstrong stayed late despite plans to go uptown, and the record became one of the biggest McRae worked on.
124.ch: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
124.q: thinking. Those guys were real deep thinkers. And Louie Armstrong never talked -- You know, one time he got mad. Just one time in his life, he got mad, when we did this -- I had to rehearse him at eleven o'clock in the night for him time to do a smash hit record (inaudible) "Don't Fence Me In with…

124.t: Dexter Gordon joins Armstrong; the "Grooving" session
124.s: The 1944 Decca sides come up; Dexter joined in California for about a month during wartime travel.
124.ch: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
124.q: Dexter just joined the band for about, oh, I'd say about a month. I don't think he stayed with us long, because he wanted to leave.

124.t: Writing Armstrong into spots rather than blowing throughout
124.s: McRae built a heavier band and spotted Armstrong in arrangements to rest his lip; Glaser objected until it worked in Canada.
124.ch: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45

124.q: And we were -- this band was built for leading up to these things we were gonna do like all those Coca-cola shows that we did.

124.t: No overseas travel; Armstrong drops the big band
124.s: McRae never went overseas in the war; Armstrong later cut the big band for an all-star group after complaining of arrangement costs.
124.ch: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
124.q: I was still working -- still doing some things with Joe Glaser, you know. And he was just -- we were talking about Louie and the ideas of things.

124.t: Delegation: Chick, Louis Armstrong and Ella left everything to him
124.s: Each leader left details to McRae, and he found that giving people departments worked best.
124.q: He worked with a straw boss and your music director. It was a lot of weight to take on all those things that he didn't --

Now the guy say, "Oh,…

124.s: McRae explains the road manager handled office business and contracts, not the band, and names Frenchie on Armstrong's tour.
124.q: Where the band is gonna stay, what time you're gonna leave. You had a road manager, but see, the road manager wasn't there to take care of the band.

124.t: Stuff Smith's band and Charlie Green's plan for Lil Armstrong
124.s: McRae had worked with Stuff Smith in 1935; Green bought Smith's band for Lil Armstrong while Louis Armstrong was in Europe.
124.ch: Depression gigs, Lil Armstrong, joining Chick Webb
124.q: "I'm thinking on buying Stuff Smath's band." Well I had played with Stuff Smith's band around (inaudible) '35 when they came down from Buffalo. They played at the Lafayette Theater.

74.t: Meeting Louis Armstrong on the St. Louis riverboat
74.s: They play opposite Floyd Campbell's band where Louis Armstrong plays; he later remembers Mosley and hires him.
74.ch: Trent's band: Texas, St. Louis and the road east
74.q: He remembered me, and that was another thrill in my life, when Louie called me up. I was with Fats, you know, but when Louie--when the Great Louie called me--I forgot all about Fats. Fats was a great band all right--

74.s: Dating when he joined Armstrong, which sessions he was on, and replacing Harry White.
74.q: Music", "Dinah", I Come From a Musical Family", "Somebody Stole My Bread", "If We Ever Meet Again"; I was on all of these records.

74.t: Writing The Man With the Funny Horn and playing it at the Missouri Theatre
74.s: He wrote the song after leaving Trent and was allowed to use the slide sax only once, in St. Louis.
74.q: St. Louis. That's the only time that they let me use 'The Man with The Funny Horn' and it broke up the place and from then on I don't remember one

74.t: Featured trombone solos and the clique in Armstrong's band
74.s: He is featured on trombone and radio broadcasts until the clique of New Orleans men turns on him.
74.q: I've got it. In that it's got my solo with--Dan's got this one--of St. Louis Blues.

74.t: Laurie Wright and a misdated paper
74.s: A London collector shows him a paper dating his record work later than he remembers.
74.q: When I got to London, Laurie Wright--I stayed out at his house for three nights. He said I want to show you something, here's the thing from the New York Age--

74.t: Quitting Armstrong and calling out the band on intonation
74.s: His solos were taken away, so he told the band they played out of tune and Louis backed him.
74.q: It wasn't exactly The Man With The Funny Horn, but it got so that I couldn't get any solos. They took most of my solos away, and in fact, I was getting pretty popular in there.

74.t: Armstrong's southern tour; never booked in Little Rock
74.s: Touring Texas and the deep South, he is disappointed not to play Little Rock.
74.q: I went to Texas--we didn't play Arkansas. We jumped from Memphis, Tennessee into Dallas and it broke my heart that we weren't booked in Little Rock. Never played there.

74.t: The Luis Russell band under Armstrong
74.s: He clarifies that he joined Armstrong's band, which was Russell's band.
74.q: No, I was in the band after Louis Armstrong took it over.

74.s: Dating his departure to spring 1937 and a newspaper item about how he quit.
74.q: You told me about that, you saw it.

74.s: Driggs sorts out which records Mosley made with Armstrong.
74.ch: Trio years, the Sands and Armstrong recollections
74.q: I did a lot of one nighters, all the way across the country.

74.t: Waiting in Kansas City while Armstrong went to Hollywood
74.s: Armstrong is away about two weeks; Mosley stays with father's family.
74.ch: Trio years, the Sands and Armstrong recollections
74.q: I had no problem at all; I was staying with my--they had a great big mansion there and I just had a ball. I was jamming a lot, I was playing my horn. Down on 18th Street, 18th and Bryant they had the Street's Hotel and we used to go down to the ballrooms and play too. We used to go everywhere.

74.t: Armstrong's trumpet section and Mosley's time in the band
74.s: Gus Aiken, Ham Davis, Louis Bacon and later Red Allen; he was in the band over a year.
74.q: They had a worse click in Louie's band than they had in Claude's.

74.s: Mosley did not like Red's playing after hearing Peanuts and they had a feud.
74.q: later, but Red was playing allright, but he didn't play no great music with that band. I didn't like his playing.

74.t: Photo of Armstrong's band without Louis
74.s: Driggs's photograph of Armstrong's men in white suits.
74.ch: Trio years, the Sands and Armstrong recollections
74.q: I haven't got a picture of me with Louie.

74.t: Red Allen, Greeley Walton and Russell Smith in the band
74.s: Red Allen arrives long after Mosley; Russell Smith plays first trumpet.
74.q: He was a terror is right. He'd get up and take a solo--I'll never forget that--we were at the Nixon Grand and (inaudible) I fell off the bandstand.

74.t: Playing Louisiana with Armstrong: no New Orleans
74.s: They play all over Louisiana but Mosley cannot recall New Orleans.
74.ch: Trio years, the Sands and Armstrong recollections
74.q: I didn't (inaudible) We played every place--we played all over Louisiana, but I don't ever remember playing in New Orleans. We played Lake Charles, Louisiana and that's where I met the Whitman Sisters and that's where Willie Bryant was with the Whitman Sisters that time.

641.t: First hearing Louis Armstrong at a Firemen's Parade

641.q: In Baton Rouge. Like I said, every parade that passed in Baton Rouge, passed in front of my house. We had a kind of a little roof on the top of my Dad's house. We lived in the... The shoe shop was in the front, and we lived in the house in the back. But anyway, I'm standing along the curb with a…

641.t: Following Louis's career and the Heebie-Jeebies record
641.s: After the parade everybody in Baton Rouge talked of Louis; Joe's first strong record memory is Heebie-Jeebies, around 1926.
641.ch: Hearing Louis and the Baton Rouge scene
641.q: But everybody, just all we could talk about was Louis Armstrong. We called him Louis. And I said, 'Well, I'm going to play with that guy one of these days.'

641.t: How the Hot Five differed from other bands
641.s: Joe says no band sounded like the Hot Five because no one else had a Louis Armstrong, though Guy Kelly had a similar combo.
641.ch: The Original Dixieland band to California
641.q: Yeah, it was different. Nobody played like that for the simple reason that nobody had a Louis Armstrong. That was one reason.

641.t: Young Men From New Orleans at Disneyland's Mark Twain
641.s: Joe turned down offers from Glaser and others to play Los Angeles clubs, then joined the Young Men From New Orleans band on the Disneyland riverboat.
641.q: Right after that... Not long afterwards... Well, this was '56. I toured around, and I got a letter from Joe Glaser that Louis wanted to sign me up and go on the road. Scovill(?) wanted me to come back with him and play with him, and different... I got a lot of offers. But I stayed here, playing…

641.t: The call from Joe Glaser to join Louis
641.s: Glaser phoned him at Disneyland while Barney Bigard was leaving; Joe gave two weeks' notice and joined Louis in Ontario in July, staying until July 29, 1964.
641.q: About a year before, I'd sat in for Barney on a couple of deals with Louis' band, and Louis told me at the time that he wanted me if Barney left. So anyway, I got this call at Disneyland...

641.t: First night in Bala, Ontario, and his feature spots
641.s: With no rehearsal, Joe played How Long Blues; Louis told him he was an All-Star and the next day asked for Yellow Dog Blues.
641.q: Of course at that time I knew Louis pretty well. Because I did a commercial with Louis that Barney didn't want to do a while back. And we had become pretty good friends just from socializing with each other. Like I said, every time he came to Los Angeles or someplace around, I was with him -- you…

641.t: The sextet and the dance dates where Louis cut loose
641.s: Joe lists Trummy Young, Danny Barcelona, Billy Kyle and the bassist; concerts grew monotonous but dances let Louis play Cornet Chop Suey and Heebie-Jeebies.
641.q: Louis... It was a terrific band in my idea, because they was...particularly at first. Then Louis' band got kind of monotonous. Because you played the same thing every night. Except once in a while we would play a dance, and that's when you heard Louis play.

641.t: Was Louis an Uncle Tom? Louis as entertainer
641.s: Joe rejects the Uncle Tom charge and calls Louis the greatest entertainer, being asked by fans if he was Louis Armstrong.
641.q: No, sir! Not by any stretch of the imagination to my idea. Louis never was an Uncle Tom. Louis was just a nice guy. Louis did all those things because he loved to do 'em, not because he was an Uncle Tom. But to me, Louis was the greatest entertainer that ever lived. He could do it all, to my idea.…

641.t: Louis as a boss: discipline and compassion toward Danny Barcelona
641.s: Louis scolded Joe for lateness and talking during solos but asked the band quietly to help Danny Barcelona rather than firing him.
641.q: Great. I made more money with Louis and I had more fun, and it was the easiest job I ever had in my life. The only trouble...one time... The only bad thing Louis ever said to me, and it wasn't bad...I mean, to warn me... I was about a minute late getting on the stand, for some reason -- I had to go…

641.t: Who ran the band: Glaser or Louis
641.s: Glaser hired and fired, but Louis named Joe himself, having wanted him since Joe's Ory days.
641.q: As far as hiring and firing guys, you had to do something (I don't know) real bad to get fired out of that band to start with. Because Louis would have the last word. But if somebody wanted to leave the band or whatever, Joe Glaser...it was up to him to hire somebody unless Louis specifically named…

641.s: Joe says Hello Dolly was his biggest hit; it was cut for Kapp on December 4, 1963, and Glaser expected You've Got a Lot of Living To Do to be the hit.
641.q: Oh, no question about it. No question about it. Because this thing was so big, you couldn't believe it. And it stayed big for a long time. The thing about it, Joe Glaser was friends with Jack Kapp of Kapp Records, and I think...

641.t: The banjo introduction dubbed on afterward
641.s: Louis disliked the take, so a banjoist brought in at Trummy's suggestion devised the introduction, dubbed in after the record was made.
641.q: they thought was really going to go was, 'You've Got A Lot Of Living To Do.' We made two sides. When we made the record, we had one little lead sheet that Louis played; it was written for Louis. And Billy Kyle scribbled a couple of little rhythm patterns. That's the only music we had. And we made…

641.t: Hearing in San Juan that Hello Dolly was charting
641.s: The band had forgotten the tune until Glaser's office called in San Juan, Puerto Rico, saying it was in the top five; the transcript ends abruptly.
641.q: So we went on tour the next day, and forgot about "Hello Dolly". This boy Bob had lost the music; he was supposed to be the band boy. And it was all forgotten until we wound up in San Juan, Puerto Rico, around Christmas. We opened in San Juan, Puerto Rico. We were supposed to be there nine days I…

641.t: Buddy Petit, Louis Armstrong and the burial of Joe Oliver
641.s: Armstrong told Darensbourg he paid for Buddy Petit's funeral, and how he found Joe Oliver running a fruit stand in Atlanta and buried him too.
641.q: Yes, sir. Louis says that, too. Uh-huh. Louis and Buddy was good friends. I was talking to Louis about Buddy not too long ago, and he's telling me when Buddy died, he said he buried him. Oh, yeah? He's the one who put up the money for his funeral.

18.t: Meeting Louis Armstrong and joining Luis Russell's band
18.s: He met Armstrong while with Luis Russell at the Savoy, and stayed with Armstrong about six years.
18.ch: Early influences, Oliver date and trombone peers

18.t: Luis Russell years into Armstrong's band, to 1940
18.s: He was with Russell 1929-31, then Armstrong took over the band; he stayed till 1940, then Cafe Society with Red Allen.
18.ch: Russell and Armstrong years, Goodman and the road
18.q: And played with Louis Armstrong. Went from Russell to Armstrong. Armstrong took over Luis Russell's band. He conducted the band until he got ready to fire Luis Russell and then he fired him (inaudible). So I stayed on with Louis until 1940. Then New Years we went down to Cafe Society with Red Allen…

18.t: Choosing Louis Armstrong over Lionel Hampton
18.s: Joe Glaser asked whom he wanted to play with and he chose Armstrong, with whom he was like a buddy.
18.ch: Family, Margaret's story and Eutris's memories
18.q: No, here's what happened, I was playing with Louis Russell and they made a decision. Louis Russell was playing in the (Apollo?) Theatre and Lionel Hampton was (there.) So Joe Glaser was back there and he asked me who did I want to play with, and I told him.

18.t: Louis Armstrong and leaving his band
18.s: Armstrong was the greatest and they were close; he gave notice to manager Joe Garland.
18.ch: Cincinnati, Buffalo, Russell and Fletcher Henderson
18.q: that I played something, always, because he and I were like this. He would sit here and I would sit here, and Lou and I were like this. We'd get the work, we'd go out, you know, to do one-nighters. He'd say, "Come on now, let's go out and sport a while." We were like that. I didn't even give him…

18.s: Allen played 30 minutes at intermissions and went over well; Allen had a funny disposition.
18.ch: Cincinnati, Buffalo, Russell and Fletcher Henderson
18.q: Yeah, during intermission. We would take intermissions and then Red would play 30 minutes with the band while we were resting.

18.t: Armstrong and Joe Glaser: early pay
18.s: Armstrong earned $750 a week at the Howard Theatre; he never heard him badly mention Glaser.
18.ch: Union, publishers, race and Harlem nightlife
18.q: Yeah, I know they liked each other. I know he paid him. Louis Armstrong didn't make all that much money when he first started.

18.t: Armstrong swearing and his wife Alpha
18.s: He heard Armstrong swear only a couple of times, and Alpha once threw coffee.
18.ch: Union, publishers, race and Harlem nightlife
18.q: he and I hang out like this. We had been out, you know, sporting around. It was too late for his wife. She threw a cup of coffee.

18.s: JCH says Armstrong and Red Allen were both Uncle Toms who took their money without saying yes sir.
18.ch: Union, publishers, race and Harlem nightlife
18.q: How so? How can anybody be one? Just an Uncle Tom, period, he and Red Allen. He worked and he got his money, but he didn't go around and say, yes sir, and you know, things like that. He didn't do that, no.

18.s: Guitarist Larry Lucie was his roommate in Armstrong's band, and they practiced daily.
18.ch: Favorite bands, advice and family reflections
18.q: Any time he knows where I'm playing. He'll do it every time. ... and we used to practice in Louis Armstrong's band practically every day. We weren't doing anything, I'd say, OK, let's play. He loved to play. And, can play.

18.s: He says Armstrong never mentioned the orphanage; Jabbo Smith and Cat Anderson came from there.
18.ch: Favorite bands, advice and family reflections
18.q: Yes. One of the best. He played trombone and trumpet and played. He played down at the Small's and let's see who else. That's about all I remember. But, every kid that came out of their orphanage played.

18.t: Louis Armstrong if he had been white
18.s: JCH thinks Armstrong has more money than Goodman; the interviewer disagrees.
18.ch: Favorite bands, advice and family reflections
18.q: Benny Goodman ain't never had much money as Louis Armstrong.

18.s: He was too sick to see Armstrong's funeral; asked about his own, he says only to give him another drink.
18.ch: Jazz opinions, Jelly Roll and the Rhythm Club
18.q: I figured they might have a band from New Orleans to play for him. But I don't know because I think I just came out of the hospital the day before or after. We were in the hospital the same time.

18.s: He was featured on Saint James Infirmary, Saints and By and By, and still features a tune Armstrong gave him.
18.ch: Cincinnati, Buffalo, Russell and Fletcher Henderson
18.q: A particular tune I feature now. This is one that Louis made and he featured me on that tune, but when I get my own band I was feature myself on it. I just like it because I made it tough. I'm not bragging on myself, you know, but made it tough for other guys to play.

94.t: Hearing Louis Armstrong through the wall of the Sunset Cafe
94.s: Outside the Sunset Cafe he heard a trumpet, learned it was Louis Armstrong, and resolved to be a jazz musician.
94.q: I'm telling you; it was rough. And when you mean rough, it means rough. It -- I always figure, figure that my ..... someday my ship will come in. And I'm beginning to, at that time beginning to see the dawn comin' up by listening in front of the Sunset Cafe and hearing this trumpet blowing through…

94.t: Karnak uniforms and the dream of joining Armstrong
94.s: Joe Glaser sent Moore to the Karnak tailor for three uniforms; he remembers the Sunset Cafe days as he went to join Louis.
94.q: Karnak was at 48th and 7th Avenue, the second floor. So I went up and in the morning they measured for three sets of uniforms --

94.t: First night and Teddy McRae's leadership
94.s: Armstrong introduced himself on the bandstand; Teddy McRae was in charge.
94.q: Of course, right away when I got on the bandstand, Louie introduced --I was to him and we got along fine, beautiful man.

94.t: What Louis taught Moore about performing
94.s: Armstrong gave subtle pointers on solos and projection; Moore says they never had a cross word.
94.q: But the job was really hard. because he had to get up early and make the two performances. So after the Zanzibar we went on tour practically all over the country, up through Canada and way out to the west coast, south -- oh, all over and so my days with Louie there was a wonderful experience. I…

94.t: The band bus and rapport with Armstrong
94.s: Armstrong rode the band bus; Moore tells how he finally told him about hearing him at the Sunset in 1929.
94.q: No, no, he always rode in tne bus. I have a lot of memories of him riding in the bus and the jokes they were telling each other and the dozens they play with each other, whenever we'd get through our performance anywhere, we can tell, all

94.t: Road manager Frenchie, the band doctor and subleaders McRae and Garland
94.s: Armstrong delegated hiring to subleaders; Frenchie handled travel and pay, Teddy McRae then Joe Garland led rehearsals.
94.q: On this tour, Louie always carried a doctor and a road manager. Whenever anybody got sick, we had the band doctor and a guy by the name of Frenchie was the road manager, he arranged transportation and hotels, paid off the boys. Many nights we got money before we even went to work because he'd get…

94.t: Getting Arvell Shaw into the Armstrong band
94.s: In St. Louis, when the bassist left, Moore recommended Arvell Shaw, and his uncle and aunt visited the Plantation to hear him.
94.q: Well, when we were in St. Louis, Uncle Bill and Aunt Mary knew I was with Armstrong and they were on their way to Arizona to visit and we timed our connection there at St. Louis because the Armstrong

94.t: Velma Middleton and eating on the road
94.s: He remembers Velma's rapport with Louis and the junk food and fruit musicians ate between jobs.
94.q: was out of this world. Velma on the records they did "That's My Desire." They sang a lot of blues together. That's Velma. I remember Velma when we played, it was in Florida, she'd get a whole bag of grapefruit, she'd be reaching up there, had it on top of the seat, she'd peel that thing and just…

94.t: Arvell Shaw's call and rejoining Armstrong
94.s: Louis played 'Some Day' for him, and Arvell Shaw called when Trummy Young left.
94.q: Well, whenever Louie went to New York, I'd always go to see him and there was a song that he played that he wrote called, 'Some Day.' And Louie knew that I loved 'Some Day,' and every time I'd go to where he was playing, he'd always tell the

94.t: Negotiating with Joe Glaser and the Bermuda debut
94.s: Glaser haggled over prices, and Moore's plunger solo on 'Wabash Blues' in Bermuda impressed Lucille Armstrong.
94.q: So I want to see Glaser and I'm in the office with Joe Glaser and Joe Glaser says to me, " I don't know, Chief, you play with the big society orchestras, I don't know if I can afford you. Do you want to play with Louie?" I says, " I always want to play with

94.s: Moore explains the Las Vegas recordings in which he played 'Some Day', though Trummy Young is on 'Hello Dolly'.
94.q: The rest of those -- here's what happened. We were booked at The Riviera in Las Vegas and we were going to be there a month, so I took the whole family out there to Las Vegas, we had an apartment and during that week or during that month we made an album and they put that "Hello Dolly" album on…

94.t: Leaving Armstrong; Tyree Glenn replaces him
94.s: Tired of travel, Moore gave notice, and Tyree Glenn took over, clashing with Billy Kyle.
94.q: Iceland, we played two or three days there and this time I think I better cut out because this is a little bit too much for me. So I had my notice in to Louie and from there we went to back to New York and we only had a few hours and we have to get warm clothes, "Where we going?" We're going to St.…

94.t: The grind of the small band and who is still alive
94.s: Moore notes the smaller band's work was a grind and discusses surviving members.
94.q: Every theatre we went in the brought 'em in world there for Louie/there was standing room only. And we got so tired from working, but it's a happy tiredness because we knew along with Louie we knew that we were liked everywhere we went and at one time Joe Darensbourg left and Eddie Shu took his…

455.t: Forty dollars pro rata and Cincinnati
455.s: The Armstrong band learns the $40 weekly pay was pro rata and stops getting paid full wages in Cincinnati.
455.ch: Chicago, Villa Venice and Louis Armstrong
455.q: We'd gone down to Texas to play. So okay, in our travels we wind up in -- well, I'm going to -- first I'm going to tell you what our salary was. We made $40.00 a week, and that was pro rata. So --

455.t: Armstrong's contract with Collins and Rockwell
455.s: Budd explains how Armstrong's lawyer Collins held power of attorney and obliged him to pay Rockwell $150 a week after his California reefer arrest.
455.ch: Chicago, Villa Venice and Louis Armstrong
455.q: So we said no, we want our whole $40.00, man. We've been out on this road, man, working with Louis Armstrong? You've got to be kidding. Well he had this guy Collins and his wife, and Collins was an old law firm in Chicago, called Collins and Collins, and how Louis got situated with Collins and…

455.t: The band strikes at Castle Farms in Cincinnati
455.s: The musicians refuse to play until paid the full $40, Armstrong waits alone at Castle Farms, then the band breaks up back in Chicago.
455.ch: Chicago, Villa Venice and Louis Armstrong
455.q: So in Cincinnati we say well, we're not going to work. We strike. We spoke to the bus driver, and he says well I got to deadhead back anyway, so anybody want to go back to Chicago is welcome to ride with us.

455.t: Armstrong splits from Collins and teams up with Joe Glaser
455.s: Armstrong learns the cost of power of attorney, tells Budd he will go with Glaser who is leaving prison, and Glaser builds an empire.
455.ch: Chicago, Villa Venice and Louis Armstrong
455.q: See? But anyway, we came on back to Chicago. Well, Louie, then, went to Europe, and him and Collins, and they got into some kind of thing, like coming back on the boat, and Collins called him a nigger, and all of that, and Louie got mad, and so Louie split from Collins, somehow or another.

455.s: Budd corrects himself that Ellis "Stump" Whitlock, not Stump Evans, was the trumpeter Louis let play 'Shine', including in Louisville.
455.ch: Armstrong band memories, Chicago players and Baltimore
455.q: Well, the reason he would write these kind of arrangements, you see, Louis sometimes, you know, he would -- he'd take along in the mission, and the rest of the band, we had to play sometimes by ourselves, without Louis. So, we had other music to play, you know. And, Stump Whitlock. That's the guy's…

455.t: "Laughing Louie" and "Sweet Sue" in the vipers' language
455.s: The band smokes before recording 'Laughing Louie', and Budd sings a chorus of 'Sweet Sue' in their made-up viper language.
455.ch: Armstrong band memories, Chicago players and Baltimore
455.q: And, we made one particular record called 'Laughing Louie'. And, Louie used to get up there and we wouldn't allow anybody on the recording sessions, you know, unless they were real personal friends, because Louie would like to get high, and he'd like for the band to get high. And, we used to -- so,…

455.t: Visiting the dying Freddie Keppard with Armstrong
455.s: On the first trip out of Chicago, Armstrong has the bus driver take the band to see Keppard, who died a week later.
455.ch: Armstrong band memories, Chicago players and Baltimore
455.q: On the -- on the -- one of our trips, you know, like, our first trip out of town, we had the bus, and we were on our way to St. Louis. And, Louis says, "Well, now, wait a minute." He says, "I want the bus driver, I want you to drive around, I'll tell you where to go, because we got to go see Freddy…

455.t: The St. Louis Vipers Club's giant joint
455.s: A St. Louis vipers club presents Armstrong with a baseball-bat-sized joint, and police guard the band's dressing room while they smoke.
455.ch: Armstrong band memories, Chicago players and Baltimore
455.q: So, anyway, we were on our way to St. Louis, and when we got into St. Louis, we got dressed and went up to play this dance. We all got on the music -- we got up on the bandstand, and they had the music racks up there. You know, all set up for us. And, when I looked on the music rack, lo and behold,…

455.t: Armstrong's 250 high C's against Hal Baker
455.s: Armstrong answers an imitation of 'Shine' by Hal Baker with 250 high C's; in Oklahoma City the band plays blind high on pot.
455.ch: Armstrong band memories, Chicago players and Baltimore
455.q: So, when we left -- we left St. Louis, we -- we played another dance in St. Louis before we left, and that was against the band called the Crackerjacks. And, Hal Baker was the trumpet player in the Crackerjacks. So, I never will forget. We took our intermission and just before we were

455.s: Budd lists the old tunes Louis played with the band, such as 'Ding Dong Daddy' and 'High Society'.
455.ch: Armstrong band memories, Chicago players and Baltimore
455.q: "Beau Koo Jack", yeah, "Ding Dong Daddy", "Mahogany Hall Stomp", you know. All of those. And, he -- he used to play "Ding Dong Daddy" then like I've never heard. "Big Butter and Egg Man". And, of course, we played all of our recordings, "World on a String", and all that stuff. But, he would go back…

455.t: Joining Louis Armstrong's band: lineup and rehearsal
455.s: Armstrong sends for Budd via Mac McKendrick; Budd lists Z. T. Randolph, Stump Evans, Keg, the Oldham brothers, Teddy Wilson and Yank Porter.
455.ch: Chicago, Villa Venice and Louis Armstrong
455.q: So anyway, while we were all living at Mrs. Otter's Mike S/ Louis Armstrong sent for us. We got a call from Mac McKendricks. Mac McKendricks was the band leader, the straw boss.

455.s: Budd and Hinton list the personnel of Armstrong's 1933 band, including Scoville Brown, Oldham brothers, Wilson, Yank Porter and McKendrick.
455.ch: Armstrong band memories, Chicago players and Baltimore
455.q: But, anyway, getting back to ZT. ZT would write this hard music, then. But, this one, this is one time he did stick us. We really just couldn't play. We had -- oh, yeah. We had Scoville Brown in the band, too.

30.t: Louis Armstrong as a bandleader and the Blue Note outburst
30.s: With Louis you could play as long as you wanted; he blew up fast and forgot, and at the Blue Note in Chicago after a fight with Lucille he griped about big-band men until Bigard answered that Whiteman's band was the worst.
30.q: You played the tune whenever you, how you -- whatever you felt and when and what tempo or anything and played as much as you want till you got tired, until you passed out if you wanted to. I mean, as long as it doesn't interfere with a schedule that they had, you know. I mean, like we'd go play…

30.t: From the film 'New Orleans' to Louis Armstrong's All-Stars
30.s: Working with Armstrong in Hollywood for the film 'New Orleans' with Zutty, Kid Ory, Bud Scott and Red Callender led to a trial at Billy Berg's, then a road tour, and the All-Stars name.
30.q: -- Billy Berg's to try out something and it went over so big, so they did another couple of weeks. So that went over big, so they said, "Well, we'll try it out on the road." So they went out on the road with the thing and it got to be big and so they called it Louis Armstrong's All-Stars.

30.t: Louis Armstrong's outspokenness and the alligator story
30.s: Louis said whatever he wished, even in the South, such as telling Tommy Dorsey 'not too slow, not too fast, just half-ass' on TV and telling a concert audience a joke about an alligator.
30.q: But Louie would say anywhere and he'd use vile language on top of that, saying that, and down south, too. Oh, God, he used to scare us sometimes. I mean, he --

30.t: Louis Armstrong's generosity and Stuff Crouch's club
30.s: Louis gave money to everyone, including Stuff Crouch, whom he set up with an after-hours club and a big Chrysler, and Crouch charged the band when they came over; Louis paid for Crouch's funeral.
30.ch: Armstrong, Big Sid and Joe Glaser
30.q: Oh, yes. Some (Unintelligible) musicians used to take him, like, for a fool. They thought he was a fool. But he used to tell me, he said, "Pops," he said, "them characters think I don't know," he said, "but I just give them poor so and so a few dollars."

30.t: Louis and the baby that was not his
30.s: Louis saved coins in a bag for the child of a woman who claimed he was the father, and Lucille told him he could not have fathered a child, which Bigard offers to show how easily he was fooled.
30.ch: Armstrong, Big Sid and Joe Glaser
30.q: He wanted a kid so bad, and -- this is real funny. He had a little gal called Sweet -- Sweetie-something and she got pregnant but not by Louie. But Louie thought it was by him because she was telling him that, you know? And, oh, he was proud. He's going to be the daddy.

30.t: Joe Glaser as Armstrong's manager and how he bought his contract
30.s: Glaser did not pay Louis's bills; he bought Louis's contract for $500 from a man who had beaten him, took abuse from Southerners for working with Black musicians, and Louis called him his father.
30.ch: Armstrong, Big Sid and Joe Glaser
30.q: Oh, he didn't have to worry about anything. He was working on a salary, like, and Joe Glaser would put the rest away for him, you know.

30.t: Glaser's salary and the IOU slips that kept Louis solvent
30.s: Louis had worked at Glaser's Sunset Cafe in Chicago before Erskine Tate, and Glaser put him on a salary with IOUs checked afterwards because his big heart gave everything away.
30.ch: Armstrong, Big Sid and Joe Glaser
30.q: Well, Joe had worked for him -- I mean, Louie had worked for Louie -- I mean, for Joe because Joe had the Sunset Cafe in Chicago and he worked for Joe for a while. Then he went with a guy named Erskine Tate at a theater called the Vendome in Chicago. And that's when this guy -- I can't think of his…

30.t: Dicky Wells working Louis for $25 above the Turf in New York
30.s: Bigard overheard Dicky Wells boast to a friend that he would show him how to get money, then win $25 from Louis with a sad story.
30.ch: Armstrong, Big Sid and Joe Glaser
30.q: Yeah. Over the -- right. And Dicky Wells brought a friend and he's telling -- and I heard him -- Louie had his dressing room. He's telling his friend, "I'll show you how to get money, man. Watch. Watch me." And he'd go in there and he puts a sad story on Louie and he thinks Louie is falling for it…

30.t: Louis wrecks his Plymouth and the tea he smoked
30.s: Louis, high on tea, ran into a bus and planned to give the wrecked car to his sister; Bigard says Crouch got him brick marijuana from Mexico, and Cozy Cole nearly crushed Louis's head after a racial insult in Europe.
30.ch: Armstrong, Big Sid and Joe Glaser
30.q: He had a little Plymouth -- and in those days he used to stay high off of tea, you know -- and he's taking it somewhere and he's driving and he's so busy talking he ran right into a big old bus, him and his Plymouth. Luckily, nobody got hurt. I said, "Now, look what you did." He said, "Oh, Pops,…

30.s: He lists Cozy Cole or Big Sid Catlett, Jack Teagarden, Dick Carey or Earl Hines, Arvell Shaw and Velma Middleton, and values having played with two of the greatest.

30.t: First meeting and hearing Louis Armstrong
30.s: He first met Armstrong in Chicago after Louis had left Oliver, and in New Orleans they knew his records, with 'Cornet Chop Suey' and Bechet's 'Wildcat Blues' heard on every street.
30.q: When I went to join King Oliver, but he had left. He used to be with King. And then when he left, the Duke joined Fletcher Henderson. That's when Fletcher came into Chicago, that's when I met Louie.

400.t: Delivering newspapers past the Sunset Cafe and watching Louis Armstrong

400.t: Louis Armstrong as the trinity of his life; peeking in at the Grand Terrace as a paper boy
400.s: Hinton, delivering papers at dawn, watched the Grand Terrace staff clean up and passed rehearsals at the old Peerless Theatre.

400.q: Well Louie was the trinity of my life. When I was 15 and delivering newspapers at 5:30 in the morning, I would go by there, peeping in the window with my paper sack on my back, seeing the waiters putting the chairs up on the tables and the black musicians with the tuxedo on and a nice cold glass in…

400.t: Brushes with Louis Armstrong in Chicago and the Oldham brothers
400.s: Hinton and other music-wrapped kids hung around Armstrong's rehearsals; friends like Budd Johnson then played with Armstrong; he did not see Louis much until 1953.

400.t: Leaving Armstrong's band to go home and Della Reese's request
400.s: Hinton leaves Armstrong to be with his daughter and returns to CBS; later Della Reese asks for him and he sends her a note.

400.q: Paid every dime of it. It was a tremendous experience working with him. And then he took a liking to me and he told me I could come see [unintelligible]. And that really did it. 418.t: Wishing he had played with Louis Armstrong's band
418.s: Morgenstern says he could have seen Dickenson with Louis after Charlie left; they mention Big Chief Moore.
418.ch: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
418.q: Oh, yeah, they got Big Chief. He played good.

418.t: Hearing Louis Armstrong, Jabbo Smith and Johnny Dunn
418.s: He first knew Louis behind blues singers; he describes Johnny Dunn's double-time playing and a long thin horn whose name he cannot recall.
