And there was one before Louis named Johnny Dunn, who I liked very much at the time. He used to the double-up time thing, you know, like the ...(? )... He'd do it with three majors and…

98.s: He recalls Armstrong and Hines playing baseball in Washington Park and the DeLisa bands playing softball against Woody Herman's team after work.
98.q: Yeah, real brotherhood, right. And that's what I liked -- I told you about Kansas City. You played there, everybody loved you. And then, this town was the same way. The guys like Louis Armstrong, that was a great sight. Louis Armstrong and Earl Hines and all of these guys out in the Washington Park…

98.t: Playing with Louis Armstrong's group and Sid Catlett at the Blue Note
98.s: He worked at the Blue Note with an Armstrong all-star band of Teagarden, Hines and Arvell Shaw, subbing for Sid Catlett.
98.q: Well, let's see, well, I told you the Woody Herman thing. And then I worked with Big Sid Catlett and Louis Armstrong's band.

98.t: Lil Armstrong's death at the Pacific Plaza tribute

98.q: Yeah. See, what had happened was, see, like the kids, when they get ready to go back to school and they were putting on this program. So I said, now, New York has done this thing for Louis Armstrong, and New Orleans has done one, so has the city of Chicago. So Louis said okay, and this was a…

98.t: Dave Peyton's band at the Regal and the shooting at Jasper Taylor
98.s: Dave Peyton's Regal band featured Reuben Reeves and Armstrong, and drummer Jasper Taylor's girlfriend once shot at him on stage.
98.ch: Chicago pioneers, community and New Orleans brotherhood
98.q: Yeah, he was the same -- see, those bands 15, 16, 17 men. And they just had a front man, he would be like the front man for them. Right, and so this is what happened. Then across the street at the Regal Theatre, they had Dave Peyton. He had his big band in there, with Rueben Reeves -- was a…

98.t: Lil Armstrong as a family friend and her Idlewild house
98.s: Lil knew him as a baby in Memphis, he visited her Idlewild country house to relax, and she loved Louis until she died.
98.ch: Pianists, Basie, Lil Armstrong and closing

98.t: Louis's managers, Lil's devotion and her death as a tribute
98.s: After Johnny Collins and Joe Glaser, Lil still loved Louis and died in a tribute to him; they compare the McPartlands.
98.ch: Pianists, Basie, Lil Armstrong and closing
98.q: Right, right, right. And, see, and then the different women, he had different wives and things. Right, so -- but during all of this, Lil still was faithful -- I mean, not faithful, but she loved him. She loved him til the end.

98.t: Lil's role in Louis Armstrong's career
98.s: DeMichael and Saunders agree Lil got Louis away from Oliver, taught him to read, ran business and set up the Hot Five.
98.ch: Pianists, Basie, Lil Armstrong and closing

98.t: Living with Lil and Louis Armstrong in Chicago
98.s: His sister was a childhood friend of Lil Armstrong, so the family stayed with Lil and Louis after they married in 1924; he recalls their late hours, the Savoy Five and its classic records.
98.ch: Childhood, first drums and the hustling years
98.q: Right, right, right, right. And then, when we first come to Chicago, in -- around '23, was the heyday of Lil Armstrong, who was from Memphis, and she and my sister were very, very close friends there, they were real buddy-buddy girls.

150.t: First seeing Louis Armstrong in Algiers in 1935
150.s: He glimpsed Armstrong in a car in 1935 and wished to meet him.
150.q: In 1935 I saw him. Where was that? I tell you he was over in Algiers. I think he went over there to talk to some friends or somebody. And it so happened that I was on, I was on Test Street and Louis Armstrong was in the automobile with somebody. And it just so happened that he stopped. And I said,…

150.t: Escorting and emceeing for Louis Armstrong in 1949
150.s: Through his press and radio work and Zulu friends he became Armstrong's driver and escort and emceed his New Orleans shows.
150.q: I don't know, it just, I tell you what happened. By being in radio and working for a newspaper, here I'm a press man. And everybody in the Zulu Club at that time, they knew me. Especially Ernest Wright who thought the world of me. I was a big name person in New Orleans because he was affiliated…

150.t: Armstrong's Secret Nine and escorting Louis Armstrong as Zulu king, 1949
150.s: Asked about Armstrong's baseball team, Tex says he did not know the players but drove for Armstrong as Zulu king in 1949, and describes the Zulu club's growth.
150.ch: Sandlot baseball and New Orleans sports
150.q: Yeah, he financed that team. Did you know any of the players in that? No, I didn't. I did not know any of the players. Because I've always looked at that photograph and I'm wondering who those players are, where of the Zulu club.

150.t: Hearing Louis Armstrong on the radio in the 1930s
150.s: He did not see Armstrong at the Astoria in 1936 but heard him on the radio from the whites-only Suburban club.
150.q: Well, yeah at that time I was 14 years of age 13, 14 years of age but I knew of Louis Armstrong and I heard him on the radio when he played the suburban club up here where they wouldn't let no blacks in it was only for white folks up here in Jefferson.

150.t: Louis Armstrong's 1965 return to New Orleans
150.s: Tex says he put Armstrong's arrival on the air in 1965, disputes that black press was shut out, and mentions Al Corbetti and changing race relations.
150.q: Did you cover that? I didn't officially cover Louis as such, but we got together and owned a couple of affairs and we had a couple of social visits, but I didn't do the writing or did the covering at that time. Other people were doing things because I was doing some other things. And if I, in 65,…

150.s: Tex and the interviewer find the original poster and read the artists listed on it.
150.q: That's it. That's it right there. Okay. I'm the one who brought that up here. Okay. That's right. That's where it come from. That's the original Jazz Fest poster right there.

150.t: Louis Messina, Andy Kirk and Tex's archive donation
150.s: Tex recalls promoter Louis Messina bringing in Andy Kirk's Clouds of Joy, and says he gave recordings to the Tulane archive.
150.q: That's right. That's a collector's item. In other words, Ted, you and me are sitting down here talking about history, the way it was and the way it should be. And for some particular reason, you still at that time had an element of people did not want to see progress between blacks and whites. You…

45.t: Buddy Petit's numbers and listening to a Louis Armstrong record
45.s: Williams tries to recall Buddy Petit's blues and Lift Em Up Joe while the two listen to a record said to be Louis.
45.q: Buddy had a number. That's right, Buddy did have a number. He used to call him Mr. Buddy, Mr. Buddy, Mr. Buddy PT. He used to call him kind of a blues, you know. Mm-hmm.

45.t: The Willow Long and Buddy Petit's influence on Louis
45.s: Williams recalls playing Sunday nights at the Willow Long as a kid and hears Buddy Petit's style and diminished endings in Louis's playing.
45.q: I went over it. Yeah, I was a kid when he was playing. I used to play at the Willow Long, up on the Willow between Josephine and Jackson, every Sunday night.

45.t: Playing at Pete Lala's with Joe Oliver's band, and growing up with Louis Armstrong
45.s: He took over Oliver's job at Pete Lala's with a small band including Armstrong, and recalls police stopping the young players and that he and Louis were born in 1900 and went to school together.
45.q: When he was at Murray and Iterville. Yeah, I worked there. When I worked there in 19, about 17, 16, I believe in part of 17. How I come to work there, Joe Oliver had the job. Well Joe Oliver went with Ory's band at that time. See, now like Saturday nights and Sunday nights he played with Ory. Well…

45.t: Louis Armstrong as a boy: charcoal, jail and learning trumpet
45.s: Williams describes Louis as a bad boy who sold charcoal, was jailed, and learned trumpet there.
45.q: No, well, you see, Lewis was a kind of bad boy, you know. See, he first was out of one thing, then another. Used to sell charcoal, had charcoal schooners on the old New Basin Canal. I guess you heard about that. But he was selling charcoal out there, you know. As a kid, you know, see. Well, he…

45.t: Street quartet singing with Red Happy and Black Benny
45.s: As kids Louis and others sang jive quartets in the street.
45.q: No, at that time, you know, he jived around. Some of him and the boys around, they walked around for D.A. Liberty, little quartets. Him and Red Happy and Black Benny and a few more of them, you know. Just jive singing. Kids, you know, like they were doing the street jazz.

45.t: Louis Armstrong's and King Oliver's numbers
45.s: Williams recalls Louis's numbers such as Wine and Grind and Sister Kate, and Oliver's blues and stock arrangements.
45.q: Louis played popular numbers too he played popular do you remember this winding and grinding yeah that was Louis number uh that's the first one I always played sister Kate's his number yeah he was it that's right sister Kate was his number Louis had a good head for making a number how did one I…

45.t: Playing at Pete Lala's with Ory, King Oliver and Louis Armstrong, 1917
45.s: After the Columbia Band, Williams sat in for Oliver's drummer at Ory's weekend job at Pete Lala's, with Armstrong also sitting in, just before Storyville closed.

You heard of Pete Lyle's? Yeah. Well, they were working there. Well, on Sunday night, Saturday and Sundays, King…

881.t: Louis and Lil Armstrong, and who wrote the tunes
881.s: He discusses Lil's lasting feelings for Louis, her death, her claim on the tune credits, and Jelly Roll Morton's recordings.
881.q: Yeah. And she fell off the pen and dead and heart attack. So I attribute that to her grieving. She never forget him. And I did have a little hassle on her. This tune strutting with some barbecue. I understand she said it was his and she said it was hers. Well you know Lil was a very good musician.…

881.t: Louis sent for him but he feared flying
881.s: Armstrong asked him to return, but he refused because of air travel.
881.q: Did you play at all during the time? No, no. Louis sent for me and I wouldn't quit. Yeah? Yeah, Louis. I had a chance to go back. Yeah, they told me they wanted to see me. How come you didn't go back? I didn't want to ride all them planes. I just started having confidence just about three or four…

881.t: Leaving for Chicago in 1917 and first hearing of Louis Armstrong
881.s: He arrived in Chicago in January 1917, recalls seeing young Armstrong at the Tulane playground in New Orleans, meeting him at his 1921 arrival, and Armstrong's promise to hire him later.
881.q: In 1917. I arrived in Chicago January the 3rd, 1917. I was thirteen years old. And it wasn't long before I began to hear them talking about Louis Armstrong. My, at the time it was Joe Oliver. I'd seen them fellas bucking one another, him and Mutt. René, I hadn't heard of René. And I hadn't heard of…

881.t: Loyalty to Armstrong, his records, and Young's Creole as first band
881.s: Jackson says Armstrong kept him in the band despite Collins, and mentions his tight playing on records and his lack of copies.
881.ch: New Orleans second line and Armstrong
881.q: They turned that down at last. Yeah. Mike comes and tells me that I'm fired. I go over to Patterson Hotel, where Louis was, and they asked him what's the matter, Louis. I said, she'll give me a notice if I'm fired. I just stick in bed and I had a lumbago. Louis says, I put you in the band and…

881.t: Back to New Orleans with Armstrong in 1931
881.s: Armstrong hired him for the band after the Showboat broadcasts, with manager troubles and a gangster threat before the Suburban Gardens run.
881.q: And I'll tell you one thing that really frightened me, and also the band. You see, in 31 we came down here and opened up at the Suburban Gardens. Well, we were broadcast from a place called the Showboat in Chicago, and they heard us, you know. So they engaged Louie to come down here and play.…

881.t: The 1931-32 Armstrong tour: Texas, Memphis jail and the Northeast
881.s: A long account of the Armstrong band tour, the Memphis jail episode, the Boston battle of bands and the disbanding.
881.q: I'd never been to drugs, that's good. I'd never been to trouble. The only time I would have been in trouble, if you may recall, they put us all in jail in Memphis, the whole band. See we played, we did six weeks and when we left, see it was supposed to be a big dance here at the end of this game…

881.t: Hearing Rene, Buddy Petit and Armstrong as a kid; Armstrong's generosity
881.s: He tells of Rene against Armstrong, the Armstrong band's high Cs, and Armstrong buying him shoes.
881.ch: Becoming a player; Rene, Bunk and Armstrong
881.q: I saw him and heard him play when I was a kid. I didn't know who he was, because I wasn't interested. All I cared during that time was to dance and follow the band. That's all I cared. You didn't know the names, man. No, I didn't know the names. I heard Buddy. Player Buddy was just starting out.…

210.t: Basin Street, the airport, statue and the camp's 'keepers of the flame'
210.s: Jacobs recalls the club named for Armstrong, praises Harris for the airport name, statue and camp, and says young New Orleans players were inspired by Louis.
210.q: Basin Street. It was named for Louis Armstrong. That’s what attracted me to Jackie Harris. Not only was she living in the city where Louis was born but she helped us get the airport name for Louis Armstrong, she helped us get the statue in the park, and she has been our representative and part of…

210.s: Jacobs describes the outpouring at his death, constant requests for his image and voice, and his pure honesty.
210.q: I would say that you can’t be emphatic enough about that. I have often thought having Satch the day that they called me to come to the office that Louis Armstrong passed, and I sat in a room where the head of every country, the head of every country, the presidents, the governors, the outpouring…

210.t: Hot Five and Hot Seven tribute at Jazz at Lincoln Center
210.s: Rowe admires the Hot Five and Seven; Jacobs announces Marsalis's tribute with cheap tickets for children.
210.q: Do you know that Wynton Marsalis is going to be doing three days of a salute to the Hot Five and the Hot Seven at Jazz at Lincoln Center in September of this year? And we succeeded in getting him to have his department market some of the tickets that can be sold for ten dollars to school children…

210.t: Armstrong did not know how loved he was
210.s: Armstrong called himself a work in progress, ignored reviews, and explained how he communicated in Africa: a note is a note.
210.q: I’ll tell you what Pops used to say, you know, he said he was a work in progress. He said I’m not finished yet. I don’t know what’s going to happen when I’m finished. So I decided I like that. I’m a work in progress. And I manage to surround myself with people I can learn from like Ms. Harris.

210.s: Jacobs describes his tape collages, ceiling collage and curiosity, including his reading about Hitler.
210.q: You know one of the things that I had to dispose of in the house must have been 14 pairs of scissors, you know little scissors that you’d cut paper dolls stuff. ‘Cause wherever Louis went he’d get a new pair of scissors or his scissors wasn’t sharp enough or something. So he’d come home with two…

210.t: How Armstrong learned so much music; origin of scat
210.s: Jacobs says music came effortlessly to Louis, who put his horn first, and describes how scat started when he lost the music.
210.q: Yes. I witnessed Louis learning. Louis’ life was music. His dedication and his passion was performing. He lived to entertain people. It was effortless for him. It was like breathing. He told his wife Lucille, who he adored, you’ve got to understand, Mama, my horn comes first, and she understood and…

210.s: Nobody chose; musicians brought songs, and Arvell Shaw's story shows Louis forgot he had recorded 'Hello Dolly'.
210.q: Nobody. Guys would bring him stuff and he would — you know like Arvell Shaw used to tell the story of being out in Denver with Louis and people are screaming for “Hello Dolly.” And Louis don’t even know what they’re talking about. So he has the band boy call me in New York asking me to send out…

86.t: Armstrong records and Louis Armstrong's Palace Theatre concert in Columbus
86.s: His coal-miner uncle's records led him to Louis Armstrong; he tells of sneaking backstage in Columbus when Armstrong hit high notes that shattered the lights.
86.q: He was a coal miner. And everyone there was a coal miner. And he used to listen to records. I think Bessie Smith was the most popular one there. And Mamie Smith. And I got interested in one that Louis Armstrong made with Bessie Smith. He made quite a few I think, him and Earl Hines and Coleman…

86.t: Armstrong's records, the Patek Philippe watch, and a record date behind him
86.s: He confirms knowing Armstrong on the records, then tells how Armstrong let him have a watch and of recording a Sy Oliver-arranged session in the 1950s.
86.q: Oh yeah, he was the only one that people listened to in those days. There was only one trumpet player, that was Louis Armstrong. And I think they had the names of each musician on the record, and it was Earl Hines, I’ll never forget, and Louis Armstrong, and Coleman Hawkins. And man, gee whiz, it…

86.t: Armstrong in the studio and at Memory Lane; older musicians as a family
86.s: Armstrong rarely needed many takes and urged Edison to play open horn; Edison talks about Basie and Ellington's long friendship and closeness among older musicians.
86.q: No, he didn’t do too many takes. He knew what he wanted to do before he got there. Evidently, he had gotten with Sy Oliver before the record date and Sy wrote the arrangements according to what Pops’ ideas were. So, we just ran through them, he didn’t take no time. It didn’t take any time at all…

86.t: Bessie Smith records and hearing Louis Armstrong
86.s: His uncle owned blues records; hearing Armstrong behind Bessie Smith at about eleven set Edison's direction, and he and Dance sort out who accompanied her.
86.q: Oh, yes, yes. All the old records of the old blues singers like Bessie Smith, Blind Lemon Jefferson. Oh, all the old Blues singers we had the records of. Then I happened to hear Louis Armstrong backing up Bessie Smith. And that's when it all started. That's for me. That's the direction I wanted to…

86.t: Louis Armstrong's range beyond the written limits
86.s: Edison explains how Armstrong hit notes above what trumpet methods said was possible, leading into his Columbus visit.
86.q: When Pops would come into town and he would be so sharp, you know. I remember before he -- you know, in his early days, you know the compass of a trumpet was from low C to a high C, and to play over this high C was absolutely impossible, like

86.t: Armstrong proves his horn at the Palace Theater
86.s: Symphony players challenged Armstrong's horn; Edison watched backstage as he played Tiger Rag with 200 high Cs and pickup bands in each town.
86.q: So they were writing that his horn was a freak horn, he had a trick mouthpiece. In those days a trumpet player could fill the little hole up with chewing gum, you know, make the hole smaller, which would enable him to play higher but then he couldn't play low, you see. So Louie Armstrong was…

86.s: Audiences everywhere spoke of Satchmo, and an Egyptian jam session showed music transcends language.
86.ch: Travels, horn and views on new music
86.q: No, they did but I’ll tell you. Every place that we went, everybody would say something about Satchmo. He’d been over there years ago, in fact I don’t think there was no place on this earth that he didn’t go. He was the greatest ambassador that ever lived for this art form, for American art form.…

127.t: Louis Armstrong: parades, Lil's teaching, and sitting in with Kansas City bands
127.s: Punch says he only worked with Louis on parades in New Orleans, with the Silver Leaf band under Frankie Dusen, where reading was not much required. 127.ch: Musicians he knew and played with
127.q: No. But what kind of brass band? Louie learned his reading from that woman he married, Lil. Lil Armstrong? Yeah, Louie got all his learning from Lil. About music, I'm telling you what I know. Well, now. But you got to give it to him. Louis was an apt fellow. Still apt. Heads, you know. Louis was so…

127.t: Coming to New Orleans to stay; Petit, Armstrong and the Army piece
127.s: After the Army he settled in New Orleans until 1926; names early trumpeters and tells of meeting Louis Armstrong.
127.q: I came here a couple of times before the war, but I didn't stay here. I went back, back in the country. But in my main time, when I came here to stay, after I left the Army. And I came on here and stood until 1926. Went on into Chicago.

127.t: Knowing Louis from the Waifs' Home before the Army
127.s: Punch first met Louis in the Waifs' Home; Louis was just a bad boy who could not yet play, and Kid Rena was there.
127.q: Sure, that's where I first met him. But he couldn't play on the horn. He was just a bad boy, you know.

127.t: Louis versus Lewis, Chicago job help and a message to Louis
127.s: Punch says they coined Satchmo, recalls Louis giving him jobs in Chicago before leaving for New York, and sends a get-well message.
127.q: Louis told me at 46... 46 in South Park, we were here in Chicago. I was ridden so much sand. I'll tell you about that. I was ridden sand. So he told me, he said, look, I'm going to give you Chicago. I said, I'm going to New York. I said, okay. I thought he was kidding me. Yeah. Man, the next thing…

127.t: Idols; Louis, King Oliver and Mama Lucy
127.s: Punch says Louis' mother was King Oliver's sweetheart, which got Louis the second trumpet job; neither taught the other, and he asks after Louis' sister.
127.q: We all was playing alike. There was no differences. And Lewis, mother, was King King. And he was a big fan of the band. And Lewis' mother was King Oliver's sweetheart. Uh-huh. See? And the woman, King Oliver, wanted a second trumpet player. So, didn't mean he or Buddy Petit and him. He said, for…

127.t: Returning from World War I and sitting in with Kid Ory at the 25
127.s: Punch returns in 1918-19 to find Louis Armstrong, Kid Ory and others at the 25; he sits in, plays army numbers and blues, and impresses the band.
127.ch: Meeting Louis and the New Orleans bands
127.q: Oh, sure. Baby Dots. And, uh... So somebody made me acquainted with Ori. I don't know who it was, but... And he asked me to come up and blow some. This is... This is no joke. This is real. So I went up and blowed. I blowed me some army numbers. I blowed me some blues, and I blowed me some songs,…

100.t: Nat as guide to Harlem and the road to meeting Louis Armstrong

Joe Marsala hired him for a big band, even though he couldn’t read music, because it was very – the parts were very easy. He got himself gigs here and there. He played in a band in Forest…

100.s: Her work on Louis's fan mail and Musicraft files, then poet and drummer Steve Tropp.

So that’s how I first got my introduction to Pops. She knew Nat very well. He had a crush on her. She was the daughter of a…

100.t: Start of the second session, March 29
100.s: Berger resumes the interview on March 29 and asks about meeting Armstrong.

100.t: Backstage with Louis Armstrong at the Roxy
100.s: Meeting Louis in his dressing room via Jeann Failows, June Clark, Joe Bushkin's rose from Tallulah Bankhead and Jack Teagarden.

100.s: Louis's gift for napping, the show with Chico Marx and the end of the day; the Army draft and his farewell party follow.
100.q: Then it was time for Louis to take his nap. Louis had a wonderful talent which I learned later, for taking naps. 100.t: Defending Armstrong and Ellington, and the Louis birthday issue
100.s: The Cavett remarks about Hawkins, requests to pay for coverage, his advocacy and the 1970 Armstrong birthday issue.

106.t: Louis offers his piano for Briggs's daughter

106.s: Briggs arranges to have the piano brought over, and describes how Louis, hurt by being pushed into retirement, fell ill and died about three years earlier.
106.ch: Asides on character, a piano and Oslo
106.q: And I -- we arranged, I sent transportation to have it brought--brought the piano here and gave her a check. And Louis was doing pretty good, but he -- I don't think he -- he was just a person who thought he was sick, imaginary sick.

106.s: In 1933 Armstrong, who discovered his manager Collins was making vastly more than paid him, left London and stayed with Pete du Conge and Bricktop at Bouchevalles.

106.s: Briggs saw pus coming from Armstrong's upper lip and attributes it to heavy pressure from overwork and lack of training, saying his playing never recovered its early precision.
106.q: And Louie stayed with her, about six -- about three months, 'cause Louie, at the time he was having a little lip trouble, too, 'cause they worked him to death.

106.q: No, 'cause he -- while we were at Bouchevalles, sometimes he would take up his horn, and try to do something, you know, for me and in my presence, and I never noticed any --

106.s: Canetti signed Armstrong and had Pete du Conge assemble his band; Briggs received a wire from Canetti but did not answer, and recalls du Conge's New Orleans clarinet background.

71.s: He recalls learning from Freddie Jenkins, hanging around Armstrong's hotel, listening to him practice and whistle, and Armstrong remembering those days.

373.s: He regrets that a backstage Armstrong interview was erased and that Herridge delayed taping Ellington's Harlem Suite on DuMont television.

80.t: Hearing Mamie Smith, Bessie Smith and Louis Armstrong on records

145.t: Louis Armstrong at Sebastian's Cotton Club

145.t: Les Hite as house band at Sebastian's; Armstrong; Hollywood visitors
145.s: Royal worked years at Sebastian's Cotton Club, where Bing Crosby and the Gus Arnheim crowd came to hear the band, which backed Louis Armstrong.

677.t: Louis Armstrong fronts the Cotton Club band
677.s: In 1930 Armstrong came to the coast alone and fronted the band; Brown calls him the most beautiful trumpeter he ever heard.

677.s: The Cotton Club band under Elkins improved when Armstrong fronted it in 1930, and Les Hite later took over.
677.ch: Los Angeles scene and the Ellington sound
677.q: Well, the band was smaller than Les Hite's band, and Elkins was -- well, he was not the musician that Les Hite was, and so therefore it wasn't up to par, we would say, and the greatest thing about the band at that time was when Louie, in 1930, came out as a solo artist and naturally he fronted the…

677.t: Bigard's unemployment claim and Joe Glaser's bookkeeper
677.s: After leaving Armstrong Bigard could not collect until an investigation found Frenchy skimming, and he received about $1,500.
677.q: -- thing, when I left Louis Armstrong and I went to get my unemployment and I put it in and because New York and California, at that time, you worked together, you know for unemployment, so when the -- you have to wait two weeks before you get it and so after two weeks I went over -- nothing for…

409.t: Phonograph records and Louis Armstrong as idol

409.q: Yes. I listened to him, but not on records. I listened to King Oliver in later years on records, but during that period of time, I only listened to Louis.

235.t: First impressions of Louis Armstrong's tone
235.s: Records at home did not strike him as a saxophone-focused youth, but as he matured he realized Louis had the most beautiful sound.

77.t: Louis Armstrong brought to Dreamland; records as Josephine Beatty
77.s: Bottoms (perhaps rather than Joe Oliver) sends for Louis Armstrong; Hunter works with Louis and Joe and records under her sister's name, Josephine Beatty.

473.t: Louis Armstrong's automatic influence on Roy and other trumpeters

13.t: Playing with Louis Armstrong at the Vendome; Jabbo Smith

957.s: The home had no band then, only a bugle played by Ike Smoot, who was killed after a dance before his band formed; Foster left about eighteen months before Armstrong arrived.

251.t: Louis Armstrong in Texas, 1931, and the Suburban Gardens

412.t: Turning down Louis Armstrong and Scobey to stay home
412.s: Hodes says Louis Armstrong's band offered him a job three times. He declined to travel and Scobey offered him a quartet instead.
412.q: Anyway, at that time she was very normal and anxious for me to know her stuff. And went over it with her and everything. Four days, I fitted right in the band. 6.q: Oh, yes, of course. Of course. I remember those records. They used to cost 75 cents. And I used to buy them. 78.t: Louis Armstrong's influence: trumpeters straining their voices and wearing handkerchiefs
78.s: After Fletcher presented Louis in Harlem, trumpet players copied his gravel voice, hung handkerchiefs and talked like him.

529.t: Louis Armstrong's band in Miami and Arvell Shaw
529.s: A new club opens with Louis Armstrong's orchestra; he gives Arvell Shaw a string and describes Miami nightclubs with floor shows.
529.q: Uh huh. Arvell broke his string. And then came around to my club and ask me for a string. And I'd go reach down in my bag and gave him a string, you know.
